exams.title: Microsoft Foundry Practitioner
exams.description: Build practical mastery of Microsoft Foundry (formerly Azure AI Foundry) — the model catalog and deployment options, building and orchestrating AI agents with Foundry Agent Service, and applying guardrails, responsible AI, security, and production operations practices. A skill track, not a certification — Microsoft Foundry is a platform you use, not a credential you sit.

lessons.title: Projects, Hubs & the Model Catalog
objectives: Structure teams as Foundry projects under a Foundry resource, and recognize when a hub-based project is still needed
Explain what the model catalog surfaces and how to compare models before deploying one

knowledgeCheck.question: A platform team at Contoso is setting up a new generative AI initiative in Microsoft Foundry and needs to decide how to structure the workspace before onboarding multiple product teams. Which structure does Microsoft recommend for new agent and model work, giving each team an isolated workspace under shared governance?
options: Hub-based projects under a shared Foundry hub
A standalone Azure OpenAI resource per team
A separate Azure Machine Learning workspace per team
Foundry projects under a single Foundry resource
knowledgeCheck.explanation: D is correct: the Foundry resource is the top-level governance boundary (networking, security, model deployments, connections) and each Foundry project is an isolated development boundary inside it, so several teams can reuse shared deployments and connections without repeated IT setup. New agent capabilities, including the generally available Foundry Agent Service, are only available on Foundry projects. A is wrong because hub-based projects appear only in the Foundry (classic) portal and are now kept for classic-only features such as prompt flow or managed compute deployments. C is wrong because an Azure Machine Learning workspace lacks the Foundry project experience for agents, evaluations and the model catalog. B is wrong because a standalone Azure OpenAI resource only serves model calls, without agent hosting or evaluations, and Microsoft provides an upgrade path from it to a Foundry resource.

knowledgeCheck.question: A platform team must onboard three product teams that need the same network and security posture, the same shared model deployments, and separate workspaces for their own agents and files. What is the main architectural benefit of putting all three teams' projects under one Foundry resource?
options: It removes the need for any network security configuration
It automatically merges all teams' data into one fine-tuned model
It centralizes governance, deployments and connections that each project can reuse
It exempts the projects from guardrail and content filtering requirements
knowledgeCheck.explanation: C is correct: the Foundry resource is where networking, security settings, model deployments and shared connections are managed, while each project is a development boundary with its own agents, files and evaluations. Teams reuse those shared settings without each one re-creating them. A is wrong because the resource is where network isolation is configured, so the work still has to be done once. B is wrong because projects keep their data isolated, and nothing merges it into a fine-tuned model. D is wrong because guardrails apply to model deployments and agents regardless of how projects are grouped.

knowledgeCheck.question: A developer wants to evaluate several LLMs — an Azure OpenAI model, a Meta Llama model, and a Cohere model — before committing to one for a new chatbot. Where in Microsoft Foundry can the developer browse and compare these models from multiple providers side by side?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: The model catalog is the central hub for browsing first-party (Azure OpenAI, Phi), partner, and open-source models (Meta Llama, Mistral, Cohere, DeepSeek, and more), including benchmarks, licensing, and supported deployment options for each.

knowledgeCheck.question: Before committing to a model for a cost-sensitive, high-volume summarization feature, a team wants to compare quality, latency, and cost trade-offs across several catalog models. Which model catalog feature directly supports this comparison?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Model benchmarks in the catalog show comparative quality, cost, and throughput/latency metrics across models on standard datasets, helping teams shortlist candidates before deployment.

lessons.title: Deployment Options, SDKs & Prompt Flow
objectives: Match a workload's traffic pattern and latency needs to the right deployment option
Distinguish the Foundry project client (azure-ai-projects) from the inference client (openai)
Explain Prompt flow's retirement and the migration path to Microsoft Agent Framework

knowledgeCheck.question: A team wants to deploy a partner model from the model catalog, whose model card lists serverless deployment, without provisioning or managing any virtual machines, paying only for the tokens they consume. Which deployment option should they choose?
options: Managed compute (real-time endpoint on a dedicated VM)
knowledgeCheck.explanation: D is correct: a serverless (pay-per-token) deployment exposes the model through an API that Microsoft hosts and manages, billed per input and output token, with no virtual machines in your subscription. A is wrong because managed compute deploys the model weights to dedicated VMs that are billed for core hours whether or not traffic arrives. C is wrong because a local ONNX export moves hosting onto infrastructure the team would have to run themselves. B is wrong because provisioned throughput reserves capacity that is billed hourly, which is the opposite of paying only for the tokens consumed.

knowledgeCheck.question: A financial-services customer needs an Azure OpenAI chat model deployment with guaranteed, consistent low latency for a real-time trading assistant and is willing to commit to reserved capacity. Which Azure OpenAI deployment type best fits this requirement?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Provisioned throughput (PTU) reserves dedicated model capacity for a customer, delivering predictable, consistent latency and throughput — ideal for latency-sensitive production workloads willing to commit to reserved units. Standard and Global Standard are shared, pay-as-you-go capacity with variable latency under load. Global Batch is for large, non-latency-sensitive asynchronous jobs processed within a 24-hour window at a discount.

knowledgeCheck.question: A developer writing Python automation needs to list a Foundry project's connections and read its project properties during environment setup, separate from making inference calls to a deployed model. Which SDK is purpose-built for these project-level setup tasks, as distinct from the SDK used for chat and embedding calls?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: C is correct: azure-ai-projects (2.x targets the current Foundry portal) provides the project client, which handles Foundry-native operations such as listing connections, retrieving project properties and enabling tracing, and can also give you an OpenAI-compatible client for model calls. A is wrong because azure-ai-inference was retired on August 26, 2026, and Microsoft's migration path for inference is the openai package. B is wrong because the openai package makes the chat completions, embeddings and Responses API calls themselves, not project setup calls. D is wrong because azure-storage-blob manages blob storage, not Foundry projects.

knowledgeCheck.question: A team wants to fine-tune a base model on their own labeled support-ticket conversations to improve response tone and format. What format must the training data file use when submitting a fine-tuning job in Microsoft Foundry?
options: A CSV file with two columns: prompt and completion
A JSONL file where each line is a conversation object with a messages array of role/content pairs
A plain .txt file with one example per paragraph
A Parquet file exported from Azure AI Search
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Fine-tuning jobs expect a JSONL file, one JSON object per line, each containing a messages array (system/user/assistant turns) matching the chat-completion message format.

knowledgeCheck.question: A team maintains a Prompt flow that chains a retrieval step, a prompt template and an LLM call, and serves it from a managed online endpoint. They are planning next year's roadmap. What does Microsoft recommend for this workload?
options: Package it as a custom model and publish it to the model catalog
Keep extending it, because Prompt flow is the main low-code tool in the new portal
Rebuild it as a Connected Agents tool in the new Foundry Agent Service
Migrate it to Microsoft Agent Framework before Prompt flow retires on April 20, 2027
knowledgeCheck.explanation: D is correct: Prompt flow is no longer recommended for new development and retires on April 20, 2027. Its runtime container images no longer receive security or package updates, and Microsoft's migration guide maps flows to Agent Framework's WorkflowBuilder, executors and edges. B is wrong because Prompt flow is a classic-only feature that the new Foundry portal doesn't offer, so extending it adds to the migration debt. C is wrong because the Connected Agents tool is not available in the new Foundry Agent Service. A is wrong because the model catalog lists models, not orchestration code, so publishing there does nothing to replace the flow.

lessons.title: Agent Service Fundamentals & Built-in Tools
objectives: Name the core Agent Service runtime components (agents, conversations, responses) and what each one persists
Choose between a prompt agent, a hosted agent, and calling the Responses API directly
Pick the correct built-in tool for a given grounding/retrieval/execution need

knowledgeCheck.question: A developer is building their first agent with the current Microsoft Foundry Agent Service and wants to understand its runtime building blocks before writing code. Which set of components powers stateful, multi-turn interactions in the current Foundry Agent Service?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: C is correct: an agent supplies a reusable model, instructions and tools; a conversation persists input and output items across turns; and a response is one unit of execution that produces output items. B is wrong because threads, messages and runs belong to the classic Agents API (built on the Assistants API pattern), which is deprecated; classic agents retire on March 31, 2027. A is wrong because those are resource and configuration concepts, not runtime conversation objects. D is wrong because those describe building a retrieval index, not an agent conversation.

knowledgeCheck.question: An agent needs to analyze an uploaded CSV of sales data, compute statistics, and generate a chart image in response to a user's question. Which built-in Agent Service tool should be enabled?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Code interpreter runs Python in a sandboxed execution environment, letting the agent load files, perform calculations, and generate outputs like charts — exactly this data-analysis scenario.

knowledgeCheck.question: A support agent should answer questions strictly grounded in a company's uploaded PDF policy documents, citing the source passages. Which tool is designed for this document-grounded retrieval?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: File search lets you attach a vector store of uploaded documents so the agent automatically retrieves and cites relevant passages when answering — the standard RAG-over-documents tool in Agent Service.

knowledgeCheck.question: A team wants their agent to call an existing internal REST API that already has a published OpenAPI 3.0 specification, without hand-writing a function wrapper for every endpoint. Which Agent Service tool is designed for this?
options: Bing grounding, since it's a general integration tool
Code interpreter, which reimplements the API in Python
File search, by uploading the OpenAPI spec as a document
The OpenAPI tool, which lets the agent call the API directly from its spec
knowledgeCheck.explanation: The OpenAPI tool lets you register an OpenAPI 3.0 specification directly, and the agent can call the described endpoints without you writing individual function wrappers.

knowledgeCheck.question: A team already has a working LangGraph agent with custom orchestration code. They want Foundry to run it with a managed endpoint, automatic scaling and a dedicated Microsoft Entra identity, while keeping their code. Which Foundry Agent Service option fits?
options: An ephemeral agent built by calling the Responses API from their own servers
knowledgeCheck.explanation: C is correct: hosted agents run your own code (for example Agent Framework, LangGraph or the OpenAI Agents SDK), shipped as a container image or a .zip of source code, and Foundry provides the managed endpoint, autoscaling, a dedicated Entra identity and observability. A is wrong because a prompt agent is defined only by configuration (instructions, model and tools), so there is nowhere to put custom orchestration code. B is wrong because a voice-based prompt agent is a managed real-time voice agent, also defined by configuration. D is wrong because an ephemeral Responses API agent runs in the team's own process, so they would host and scale it themselves.

lessons.title: Multi-Agent Orchestration & RAG
objectives: Decide when a problem justifies multiple agents instead of one agent with more tools
Choose between Foundry workflows, the A2A tool, and Microsoft Agent Framework for a given orchestration shape

knowledgeCheck.question: An enterprise is moving a classic 'triage' agent to the new Foundry Agent Service. The classic version used the Connected Agents tool to hand work to a 'billing agent' and a 'technical-support agent', each with its own instructions and tools. What does Microsoft recommend for agent-to-agent delegation in the new Agent Service?
options: Use the A2A tool or a multi-agent workflow
Keep the Connected Agents tool, which works unchanged in the new API
Merge both specialists into one agent's instructions
Expose each specialist as a file search vector store
knowledgeCheck.explanation: A is correct: the Connected Agents tool from the classic Agents API isn't available in the new Foundry Agent Service. Microsoft recommends the A2A tool, which calls any A2A-compatible endpoint (including another Foundry agent exposed as an A2A endpoint), or a workflow that orchestrates several Foundry agents declaratively. B is wrong because the migration guide lists Connected Agents as unavailable in the new API. C is wrong because merging the specialists throws away the separate instructions, tools and guardrails that made the split worthwhile. D is wrong because a vector store holds documents for retrieval and can't run another agent.

knowledgeCheck.question: A team wants to build, in its own Python code, a research assistant where planner, researcher and critic agents work over several rounds to refine an answer, with explicit control over the execution path. Which Microsoft framework is designed for this code-first multi-agent orchestration?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: A is correct: Microsoft Agent Framework is the direct successor to Semantic Kernel and AutoGen, built by the same teams. It combines AutoGen's agent abstractions with graph-based workflows that give explicit control over multi-agent execution paths, in Python and .NET. B is wrong because Prompt flow is retiring and was built for chaining LLM steps, not for agents conversing over several rounds. C is wrong because Connected Agents was a classic-only Agent Service tool for simple delegation, and it isn't available in the new Agent Service. D is wrong because Azure AI Search is a retrieval service, not an orchestration framework.

knowledgeCheck.question: A .NET team built its agent on Semantic Kernel, exposing existing application functions to the model as plugins, and wants to align with Microsoft's current agent framework for new work. What is the recommended path?
options: Rewrite each plugin as a Prompt flow Python node
Migrate to Microsoft Agent Framework using the Semantic Kernel migration guide
Wrap each plugin as a Connected Agents tool
Stay on Semantic Kernel, because Agent Framework only supports Python
knowledgeCheck.explanation: B is correct: Microsoft describes Agent Framework as the next generation of both Semantic Kernel and AutoGen, and publishes a migration guide from Semantic Kernel. Agent Framework keeps enterprise features such as session-based state, middleware and telemetry, and registers functions as tools. A is wrong because Prompt flow retires on April 20, 2027 and is not an agent framework. C is wrong because the Connected Agents tool delegated to other agents rather than exposing functions, and it isn't available in the new Agent Service. D is wrong because Agent Framework supports .NET and Python, with Go in public preview.

knowledgeCheck.question: A team building a RAG-enabled agent chooses to manually construct their retrieval pipeline (outside the File search tool) for finer control over chunking and embeddings. Which two steps are essential when preparing documents for a custom RAG index in Azure AI Search?
options: Compress files and encrypt them with a customer-managed key
Fine-tune the base model on the raw document text
Convert all documents to CSV and assign an agent ID
Chunk the documents into passages and generate vector embeddings for each chunk
knowledgeCheck.explanation: A custom RAG pipeline needs documents split into retrieval-sized chunks and each chunk embedded into a vector representation so the search index can perform vector/hybrid similarity search at query time.

knowledgeCheck.question: An architect is deciding whether a customer-support use case needs a single agent with several tools, or a multi-agent design (for example, a Foundry workflow or agents connected through the A2A tool). Which factor most strongly favors a multi-agent design over a single agent with many tools?
options: The task naturally decomposes into distinct specialist roles (e.g., billing vs. technical triage) each needing different instructions, tools, and guardrails
The team wants to minimize the number of API calls at any cost
The use case only ever needs code interpreter
The team has no budget for additional model deployments
knowledgeCheck.explanation: A is correct: multi-agent designs pay off when the problem splits into specialist roles that each need their own instructions, tools and guardrails; a single generalist agent with many tools gets harder to control as its scope grows. B is wrong because adding agents usually adds model calls and hops, so minimizing calls argues for one agent. C is wrong because a use case that needs only code interpreter is a single-tool job with nothing to decompose. D is wrong because each extra agent adds model usage and operating overhead, so a tight budget argues for staying with one agent.

lessons.title: Content Safety & Evaluation
objectives: Match a failure mode (harmful content, injection, hallucination, IP recitation) to the right Content Safety capability
Explain the difference between quality evaluators and risk/safety evaluators
Explain how guardrails apply to agents, including the tool-call and tool-response intervention points

knowledgeCheck.question: An attacker embeds hidden instructions inside a document that a RAG agent retrieves and summarizes, attempting to make the agent ignore its original instructions. Which Azure AI Content Safety capability is designed to detect this kind of attack?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Prompt Shields detects both direct jailbreak attempts in user input and indirect prompt injection hidden in third-party content (documents, tool/plugin outputs, emails) that the model processes.

knowledgeCheck.question: A team's RAG chatbot occasionally states facts not present in the retrieved source documents. Which capability is designed to flag this kind of ungrounded (hallucinated) output relative to the provided source content?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Groundedness detection compares generated text against the provided source/grounding documents and flags claims not supported by that source — the standard tool for catching RAG hallucination.

knowledgeCheck.question: A model deployment uses a guardrail that blocks Violence at the High level on user input and output. An agent built on that deployment is assigned its own custom guardrail with Violence at Low for user input and output, and no controls for tool calls or tool responses. How is Violence detected for this agent?
options: The model's High setting applies, because the stricter guardrail always wins
The agent's guardrail fully overrides the model's: Low on input and output, and tool calls and responses aren't scanned
Both guardrails are merged, so input and output are scanned at High and tool calls at Low
Tool calls and tool responses inherit the model's High setting automatically
knowledgeCheck.explanation: B is correct: in Foundry, an agent's risks are detected according to the guardrail assigned to the agent, which fully overrides its model's guardrail. With Violence at Low on input and output and no tool-call or tool-response controls, user queries and final outputs are scanned at Low and tool traffic isn't scanned for Violence. A is wrong because there is no stricter-wins rule; the agent guardrail replaces the model one. C is wrong because the two guardrails aren't merged. D is wrong because tool-call and tool-response scanning only happens if the agent's guardrail includes controls for those intervention points.

knowledgeCheck.question: A team wants an automated numeric score for how well their RAG chatbot's answers align with retrieved context, how coherent the text is, and how fluent the language is, across a test set of 200 Q&A pairs. Which Microsoft Foundry capability provides this kind of automated scoring?
options: Built-in evaluators (e.g., groundedness, coherence, fluency, relevance)
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Microsoft Foundry's built-in evaluators compute standardized metrics like groundedness, relevance, coherence, fluency, and similarity over a dataset of generated responses.

knowledgeCheck.question: A security team wants to systematically probe their deployed agent with adversarial prompts to discover jailbreaks before a red-team engagement, using an automated, repeatable process integrated with Microsoft Foundry. Which capability supports this automated adversarial testing?
options: The AI Red Teaming Agent / PyRIT integration
knowledgeCheck.explanation: The AI Red Teaming Agent in Microsoft Foundry builds on PyRIT (Python Risk Identification Tool) and Foundry's risk and safety evaluations to automate adversarial probing — running attack strategies against a model or agent and reporting metrics such as Attack Success Rate (ASR).

lessons.title: Security, Privacy & Operations
objectives: Apply least-privilege role assignment to a real access-scoping scenario
Explain the difference between network-level isolation and identity-based authorization
Describe the Discover → Protect → Govern approach to responsible AI

knowledgeCheck.question: A security review flags that an application currently authenticates to its Microsoft Foundry endpoint using a long-lived API key stored in application configuration. What is the recommended alternative to reduce secret-management risk?
options: Rotate the same API key more frequently
Authenticate using Microsoft Entra ID-backed managed identity instead of an API key
Embed the key directly in client-side JavaScript for convenience
Disable authentication entirely for internal traffic
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Managed identity lets the application authenticate via Microsoft Entra ID without any stored secret, eliminating the risk of key leakage or the operational burden of rotation.

knowledgeCheck.question: A platform team is assigning permissions so that developers can build and test agents in an existing Foundry project, but must not create projects, deploy models or grant other users access. Which built-in role assignment follows least privilege for these developers?
options: Foundry User on the Foundry project
Azure AI Developer on the Foundry resource
Foundry Account Owner on the Foundry resource
knowledgeCheck.explanation: B is correct: Foundry User (previously named Azure AI User) grants reader access plus the data actions needed to build and develop in a project, but can't create projects, manage models or assign roles. Microsoft calls it the least-privilege role for developers building and testing agents. A is wrong because Owner can assign any role to anyone, far beyond the requirement. C is wrong because Azure AI Developer is scoped to Azure Machine Learning workspaces and Foundry hubs, and Microsoft says not to use it for Foundry projects. D is wrong because Foundry Account Owner can create projects, manage models and assign roles.

knowledgeCheck.question: A healthcare customer's compliance team requires that the Foundry resource and the resources it connects to never be reachable from the public internet. Which networking configuration achieves this?
options: Enabling public network access with IP allow-listing only
Disabling public network access and using private endpoints on the Foundry resource and each connected resource
Relying solely on Content Safety filters
Using a shared API key with a long expiration
knowledgeCheck.explanation: B is correct: disabling public network access and adding private endpoints keeps traffic to the Foundry resource off the public internet. Connected resources such as Storage, Key Vault and Azure AI Search are separate Azure resources with their own governance boundaries, so their networking has to be locked down too. A is wrong because IP allow-listing still exposes a public endpoint, just a restricted one. C is wrong because content filters moderate what the model says, not who can reach the network. D is wrong because an API key is an authentication choice, and a long-lived shared key adds risk rather than removing exposure.

knowledgeCheck.question: A financial institution's data-protection policy requires that encryption keys for data at rest be fully controlled and rotatable by the customer, not Microsoft. Which Microsoft Foundry capability satisfies this requirement?
options: Customer-managed keys (CMK) stored in Azure Key Vault
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Customer-managed keys let the customer supply and control the encryption key (via Azure Key Vault) used to protect data at rest, including rotation and revocation.

knowledgeCheck.question: A new team lead asks for a one-sentence summary of how Microsoft organizes its responsible AI recommendations for Microsoft Foundry agents, to include in a governance deck. Which stages does Microsoft use to organize these recommendations?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: B is correct: Microsoft's responsible AI guidance for Foundry follows the Microsoft Responsible AI Standard pattern of Discover (find quality, safety and security risks before and after deployment, for example with adversarial testing), Protect (guardrails and content filters at the model and agent level) and Govern (tracing, monitoring and compliance integrations in production). Older Microsoft guidance used a four-stage Identify, Measure, Mitigate, Operate framing; the current docs use the three stages. A is wrong because it describes a generic delivery pipeline. C is wrong because it describes a code-review workflow. D is wrong because it describes a data and model-training pipeline.
